_comment: Lars Demo Video - IJCAI 2026 Demo Track
_version: 13.0 - IJCAI timing cut: fast intro + compressed prompt engineering
_design_principles: Live collab with a real second browser
Dialogue style: Alex (Lars expert) explains, David (reviewer perspective) asks smart questions — viewer should identify with David

guest.name: David
guest.description: A reviewer persona who has read the paper and asks practical questions — the audience should identify with him

_tts_naming: TTS models say 'Lars' (without the leading L) because they mispronounce 'Lars'. In all written text, overlays, and UI, the correct name is 'Lars'.

steps._section: === INTRO (35s) — Fast problem framing and login ===
steps._concept: Alex and David introduce themselves. Alex states the core problem and triggers the merge animation exactly when saying Lars.
steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Hi, I'm Alex. Today I'm joined by my colleague David.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: Hi, I'm David. I read the paper and I'm curious what you'll show me today.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: There is still a gap between quality goals and technical implementation in LLM projects. LARS solves this gap by bringing everyone into one shared workflow.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: Makes sense, I understand.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: Sounds good, Alex. While you log in, I'm following along.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Here's the pipeline. Teams start in Prompt Engineering, where domain experts and developers co-author prompts together in real time. Those prompts feed into Batch Generation, which runs them across multiple models and datasets. And everything flows into Evaluation, where humans and LLMs assess the outputs side by side — with live agreement metrics.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: We start in Prompt Engineering, where domain and technical experts work on one shared prompt.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: I'll create a fresh prompt and share it with a second reviewer account so we can edit it live together.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: First I name the prompt, then I add ijcai_reviewer_2 as collaborator in the share field.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Great, the prompt is shared now. David, open the collaboration browser, sign in as reviewer two, and open the shared prompt.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: Ah, I see. So we can really work on the same prompt in real time while you set up the blocks.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Exactly. Now I fill the blocks and insert variables for subject and content.

actions.text: You are a counselling assistant that extracts key facts from psychosocial counselling communication.
Read the email thread and write a short situation summary in 2 to 3 sentences. Focus on family situation, health, and main concerns.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: These braces are template variables. I add sample values so we can test immediately.

actions.text:
Client wrote:
My 14-year-old son has refused school for three weeks and reports headaches. The teacher mentioned social exclusion.

Counsellor wrote:
School refusal can indicate stress and possible bullying. Arrange a meeting with the school counsellor and define next support steps.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: I'm logged in. I'll add one clarification about the data format from my side.

actions.text: The fields come from one counselling case: subject line and full message thread.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Great. One click on Test, variables are injected, and we immediately review the output.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: David is editing in the second browser now, and changes appear live on my screen. The version panel tracks who changed what.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Perfect. We now have the live co-authored prompt and a second pre-seeded prompt. We'll compare both in Batch Generation.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: We've connected our own Mistral and Magistral models, but any user can bring their own. Let me quickly add OpenAI.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: I'll add OpenAI — select the type, paste the API key, pick GPT-5 Nano and GPT-5 Mini, and save.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: Can I share this provider with my colleague so they can also use these models?

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Absolutely — your API key stays private, but others can use the models. Let me share it with IJCAI Reviewer 2.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: So we have two prompts now. What's the next step — how do we actually run them against data?

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: That's where Batch Generation comes in. We create a job that runs our prompts against a dataset with multiple models at once.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: First, the data: ten counselling cases in JSON. Lets look at the JSON structure, here ist the subject, and the corresponding content.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: I understand. Let's set it up.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Lars maps those fields automatically. I'll paste the JSON into the wizard.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: And now we pick which prompts to use? I see both our prompts listed here.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Yes you are right, I selected both. Next we pick models. I'll take Mistral Small — one of our connected open-source models — and GPT-5 Nano from OpenAI, so we can compare providers directly.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: I'll name this job and we can review the full configuration.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: Ah, here I see the generation matrix, this is a Cartesian Product, right?

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Yes, ten data points, times two prompts, times two models — forty situation descriptions total. And notice the cost estimate — Lars calculates expected tokens and cost before you run anything.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: While that job runs in the background, let me open a completed batch so we can look at the actual outputs.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: Ah, here I see how it looks after the Batch Generation is done. Can we look at one of these outputs in Detail?

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Yes of course. Here's the full trace — rendered prompt on the left, model output on the right, plus metadata. The provenance is fully tracked — you always know which prompt and model produced each output.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: OK — so we have forty situation descriptions now. Mistral versus GPT-5 Nano, each with two prompts. But how do I as a reviewer decide which combination actually works best?

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: From a completed batch, we can open the Scenario Wizard right away.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: For cross-model comparison, we choose Ranking — specifically Bucket Ranking.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: Bucket Ranking — so instead of sorting all four items into one long list, I just drop them into categories like Good, Medium, and Poor?

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Yes you do. Evaluators place each item into one bucket, so they avoid forced full ordering.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: And below that, we configure assignment and randomization.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: Great. So I can choose full overlap or split items across evaluators, and still keep random order?

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Yes, as you want. Next we add ourselves as human evaluators. For LLM-as-Evaluator, I'll pick Magistral and GPT-5 Mini.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: And we create the scenario. We actually set one up earlier with completed evaluations — but first, let me show you what evaluation looks like from the evaluator's perspective.

steps._section: === HUMAN EVALUATION (30s) — Show bucket ranking from evaluator perspective ===
steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: From the scenario workspace, I'll go back to Home via the Lars logo and open the Evaluation module. In this evaluator view, each assigned scenario appears as a card.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: These are the ten counselling cases? Each with four situation descriptions to rank. Ah, I see those are the situation descriptions we just generated with the Batch Generation.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Here you see bucket ranking, the default evaluation mode in Lars. Instead of a full ordering, evaluators drag items into quality categories. Notice the generic labels — Item A, B, C — so model and prompt identity stay hidden.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: That's much easier than sorting everything into one long list. And it's completely blinded — no model names?

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Yes, no model names, no prompt labels, and every evaluator sees items in a different random order. Unbiased by design. Now let's switch to the scenario owner's perspective and look at the aggregated results.

steps._section: === SCENARIO MANAGER (60s) — Overview, Data, Team briefly, then Evaluation with provenance focus ===
steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: In the Scenario Manager, here's is the pre-built scenario at which we just look. Here both IJCAI reviewers and two LLM evaluators have been ranking.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: The Overview tab shows live progress — how many rankings each evaluator has completed. Human reviewers and LLM evaluators appear side by side.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: In the Data tab, we can open each individual data point. I click the eye icon on one thread, and now we see the full item with its messages and how it was evaluated.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: And the Team tab — you can add or remove human evaluators and LLM-as-Evaluators at any point, even mid-evaluation.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: Humans and LLMs as first-class evaluators in one list — nice. But where do I see the actual results?

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: In the Evaluation tab. Up top we see agreement metrics — Krippendorff's alpha and others. Here, this All-Human-LLM toggle lets you switch between All, Human only, and LLM only evaluation views.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: But the key outcome is the provenance analysis. Since batch generation tracks which model and prompt produced each output, we trace evaluation ratings back to their source. This view ranks every model-prompt combination by how often its outputs land in the top bucket — and you see the best-performing pair right here.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: So this directly tells me which model and prompt pair to deploy? That's exactly the question you started with!

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Yes — and there are separate views per model and per prompt, plus a full bucket distribution for each combination.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: The agreement heatmap shows pairwise evaluator agreement — green means high, red means low. You can immediately spot where humans and LLMs disagree. Let me click a cell.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: A per-item breakdown — so you can pinpoint exactly which cases caused disagreement?

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: And if disagreement is systematic, you refine the prompt and run another evaluation. That's the iterative loop. Everything is exportable as JSON or CSV.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: We showed this with counselling data because that's our research domain — psychologists and social workers use Lars to craft prompts for extracting situation descriptions from client communications. In interviews, domain experts told us Lars eliminates the translation work between disciplines. But the platform is domain-agnostic — swap the email threads for medical reports or legal documents, and the workflow stays the same.

steps.speaker: guest
steps.narration: That walkthrough was excellent. I'll log in again and go through everything once more on my own.

steps.speaker: moderator
steps.narration: Thanks David. Lars is open-source — the credentials are on screen if you want to try it yourself. Check the repo and let us know what you think!
